item.text: {"text":"Sampled softmax offers a practical ranking objective, but sampling distribution and correction matter. [Correcting the LogQ Correction (RecSys 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331) identifies a flaw in conventional correction: the positive target is always included, whereas negatives are sampled. Its revised objective corrects negative sampling separately and weights examples by model uncertainty. This addresses sampling bias, not whether an unobserved item is actually a false negative. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) compares uniform, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling; aggregate gains conceal substantial head/mid/tail trade-offs, with popularity-based negatives sometimes improving balance while reducing overall accuracy.\n\n[CATS (SIGIR 2026)](https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1775773) directly addresses false negatives and includes BERT4Rec experiments. It uses item-embedding clusters and Thompson sampling to balance exploration and hardness, gradually reducing sampling from the positive item’s own cluster, where suspected false negatives concentrate. Its reported gains concern other datasets, so transfer to Industrial_and_Scientific and Electronics remains unproven. Practical hypothesis: retain the masked-target BERT4Rec backbone and compare uniform sampled softmax against a controlled mixture of random and same-model hard negatives; exclude known training positives and avoid concentrating exclusively on the highest-scoring candidates. Treat sampling correction and false-negative control as separate ablations. Preserve appended-mask inference and one checkpoint per category; select by the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10, since larger training margins alone do not establish improvement."}
